claim: Semantic entropy, averaged across 30 combinations of tasks and models, achieves an AUROC of 0.790, outperforming naive predictive entropy (0.691), a P(True) self-check baseline (0.698), and an embedding-regression baseline (0.687).
stance_target: sampling-based semantic clustering outperforms simpler token-probability and self-check confidence baselines
scope_conditions: 30 task x model combinations; LLaMA, Falcon, Mistral families, 7B-70B parameters; general QA and math, not code
quoted_support: Averaged across the 30 combinations of tasks and models we study, semantic entropy achieves the best AUROC value of 0.790 whereas naive entropy (0.691), [P(True)] (0.698) and the embedding regression baseline (0.687) lag behind it.

claim: Semantic entropy performance is stable (AUROC between 0.78 and 0.81) across different model families (LLaMA, Falcon, Mistral) and parameter scales (7B to 70B), and outperforms baselines across all model sizes.
stance_target: semantic entropy is a robust, scale-invariant sampling-based confidence signal
quoted_support: Semantic entropy performs well consistently, with stable performance (between 0.78 and 0.81 AUROC) across the different model families (LLaMA, Falcon and Mistral) and scales (from 7B to 70B parameters) which we study.

claim: A 'discrete' semantic entropy variant approximates the entropy directly from the number of generations falling into each semantic cluster (via the law of large numbers), rather than from token-level probabilities, and performs similarly to the probability-based estimator in practice; it is usable when internal token probabilities are unavailable.
stance_target: clustering-count-based estimators can substitute for probability-based semantic entropy without much loss
scope_conditions: general QA/biography datasets in the paper
quoted_support: Discrete semantic entropy approximates [the entropy] directly from the number of generations in each cluster, disregarding the token probabilities... We find that discrete semantic entropy results in similar performance empirically.

claim: On a GPT-4 paragraph-length biography dataset (150 manually labeled factual claims across 21 individuals), discrete semantic entropy outperforms a self-check baseline and a paragraph-adapted P(True) baseline on both AUROC and AURAC, though P(True) narrowly edges ahead once more than 20% of the most-likely-confabulation answers are rejected.
stance_target: semantic entropy generalizes beyond short-answer QA to longer free-form generation
scope_conditions: GPT-4 (v.0613) biography generations for 21 individuals, 150 factual claims
quoted_support: Discrete semantic entropy has better rejection accuracy performance until 20% of the questions have been rejected at which point [P(True)] has a narrow edge.

claim: The canonical semantic entropy evaluations use TriviaQA, SQuAD 1.1, BioASQ, SVAMP (math word problems), and NQ-Open -- general knowledge QA and elementary math -- with no code-generation dataset included, leaving a domain gap for code-LLM validation.
stance_target: coverage gap in canonical semantic entropy work relative to code-generation confidence calibration
scope_conditions: datasets used in Farquhar et al. 2024 experiments
quoted_support: BioASQ is a life-sciences question-answering dataset... SQuAD is a reading comprehension dataset... TriviaQA is a trivia question-answering dataset. SVAMP is a word-problem maths dataset... NQ-Open is a dataset of realistic questions aggregated from Google Search.

claim: Semantic entropy is unsupervised, requires no labeled confabulation examples, no task-specific training data, and no architectural modification to the LLM, but does require sampling multiple generations per prompt at test time to build semantic clusters -- the exact cost that single-pass approximations (SEPs, Dist2ill) target.
stance_target: sampling-based confidence is accurate but expensive due to multi-generation requirement
quoted_support: It can be applied directly to any LLM or similar foundation model without requiring any modifications to the architecture... Our method is unsupervised, meaning that we do not need labelled examples of confabulations.

claim: Semantic entropy detects 'confabulations' specifically -- arbitrary, ungrounded generations -- but does not guarantee overall factuality, and does not address other error types such as consistent errors learned from training data.
stance_target: scope limits of semantic-entropy-based hallucination detection
quoted_support: However, it does not guarantee factuality because it does not help when LLM outputs are systematically bad... this also includes other types of mistakes for which semantic entropy is not suited, such as consistent errors learned from the training data.
